title: American Ghost Stories
author: F. Marion Crawford, Ambrose Bierce, Ellen Glasgow and others
written: Between 1878 and 1925, mostly for magazines and annuals, by ten writers of whom seven are women
setting: A liner's state-room, a surgeon's house, a Vermont farmhouse, a family study, a plains ranch, early San Francisco and a snowbound farm
lengthNote: Ten complete stories, 1878 to 1925, with six parts of essays on the magazines, publishers and editors that carried them
openingLine: Henry had words with Edward in the study the night before Edward died,
summary: Ten American ghost stories from the half-century when the magazines ran on them. Crawford puts something cold and wet in the upper berth of a transatlantic liner; Bierce introduces his haunted house in the voice of the local paper; Glasgow's nurse and Freeman's three sisters see what the men of the house would rather they didn't; and Olivia Howard Dunbar tells her story from the other side, as a dead wife watching her husband and her sister fall in love. Seven of the ten writers are women, and the edition's essays follow how the stories were bought, edited and kept in print.
referenceStyle: story title, with the copy-text named at the head of each story

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of Famous Modern Ghost Stories, ed. Dorothy Scarborough (eBook 15143)
sourceText.note: Scarborough's 1921 anthology, the copy-text the Astor edition uses for Bierce and Dunbar, and which also prints Freeman's story. The quotations here all come from those three; the other seven are described.

atAGlance.label: Ten stories
atAGlance.note: From Emma Frances Dawson's An Itinerant House to Edith Wharton's Bewitched.

atAGlance.label: Ten writers
atAGlance.note: Dawson, Wynne, Peattie, Freeman, Dunbar, Glasgow and Wharton, beside Crawford, Bierce and White.

atAGlance.label: Where they ran
atAGlance.note: Harper's, Everybody's, Pictorial Review and a Christmas annual among them; the essays follow who bought what.

atAGlance.label: Copy-texts
atAGlance.note: Every story is headed by the edition it is printed from, with its spelling and punctuation kept.

structure.label: Crawford, White and Bierce
structure.title: Travellers and strangers
structure.summary: Three stories about men away from home. Crawford's is an after-dinner yarn about a state-room nobody should sleep in; White's motorist crashes on a country road at dusk; Bierce's stranger arrives by stage-coach, takes offence on a hotel porch and agrees to a duel with knives in the dark.

scenes.title: State-room 105
scenes.summary: A passenger is warned that on the last three trips whoever slept in 105 went overboard; he wakes to find the porthole open and the cabin smelling of stagnant sea-water.

scenes.title: The boy by the road
scenes.summary: A motorist swerves at a stone that seems to have changed sides of the road, wrecks his car, and is met by a silent farm boy with a harelip.

scenes.ref: The Middle Toe of the Right Foot (1890)
scenes.title: The Manton house
scenes.summary: Three young men set up the duel as a trick on the stranger; next day the sheriff finds him dead of fright in a corner, with footprints in the dust.

structure.label: Wynne, Peattie and Dawson
structure.title: Houses that come and go
structure.summary: Three stories in which the building itself is in question. In Wynne's Vermont farmhouse some visitors find a little room with a blue chintz lounge and a pink shell, and others find a china-closet. Peattie's young bride on a plains ranch can see a neighbour's house that her husband says is not there. Dawson's San Francisco is a city whose streets are blocked by houses being moved.

scenes.title: Room or closet
scenes.summary: Two generations visit the same farmhouse and cannot agree whether the little room is there.

scenes.title: Across the corn
scenes.summary: When the corn is cut, Flora sees a cottage to the west with smoke from its chimney. Bart tells her what happened there and that it burned.

scenes.title: The roving house
scenes.summary: The earliest story here, told among lodgers in early San Francisco, where houses were moved from street to street.

structure.label: Glasgow and Freeman
structure.title: Women who see what the men deny
structure.summary: Glasgow's nurse, hired by a surgeon she adores to sit with his wife, keeps seeing the wife's small daughter, and is then told the child is dead. Freeman's three sisters sit in the family house where their brother Edward lies dead and watch a shadow on the study wall that looks like him, while their other brother, the doctor who put the death down to gastric trouble, tries to explain it away.

scenes.title: The child in Scotch plaid
scenes.summary: Miss Randolph sees a little girl with a ball in the Maradick house; the wife believes her husband killed the child.

scenes.title: The study
scenes.summary: Whenever a lamp is set on the study table the shadow appears on the wall, and no moving of the furniture shifts it.

structure.label: Dunbar and Wharton
structure.title: The dead who stay
structure.summary: The collection closes with its two strangest stories. Dunbar's Shell of Sense is narrated by Frances, a dead wife who stays in her house, watches her husband and her sister fall in love, keeps them apart, and finally brings them together. In Wharton's Bewitched, the latest story here, three neighbours are summoned through the snow by a farmer's wife who says her husband is meeting a dead girl at a shack on Lamer's pond.

scenes.title: The narrator
scenes.summary: A ghost's account of her own house, the small wrongs in it, and the jealousy she has to give up.

scenes.title: Lamer's pond
scenes.summary: Orrin Bosworth, Deacon Hibben and Sylvester Brand hear Mrs Rutledge out; the girl she names is Brand's dead daughter, Ora.

characters.name: Frances
characters.role: The narrator of The Shell of Sense, dead and still in her house
characters.summary: She comes back to find the room intolerably unchanged, then notices the small wrongs: windows shut too tight, her work-basket in disorder, her sister at her desk. Jealous, she keeps her husband and her sister apart for months, then makes one last great effort to bring them together.
characters.clue: Notices that the gaps she left in her own bookshelves have not been filled.

characters.name: Theresa
characters.role: Her sister, living on in the house
characters.summary: She answers the condolence letters at her dead sister's desk and has never minded disorder. She loves Allan, gives him up for her sister's sake and prepares to leave the house; the story's ending depends on her being decent.
characters.clue: Wakes when the clock strikes one, certain her sister's kiss is on her cheek.

characters.name: Allan
characters.summary: A sceptic with, in his wife's words, hard and fast denials of the invisible, who feels a chill in the room he cannot account for. In the night Frances comes to him with a message: don't let Theresa leave, take her and keep her.
characters.clue: Says he can never understand, but he knows.

characters.name: The Glynn sisters
characters.role: Caroline, Rebecca Ann and Emma (Mrs Brigham), in The Shadows on the Wall
characters.summary: Three sisters in black in the family house where their brother Edward lies dead. They suspect their brother Henry and will not say so aloud. Freeman lets their conversation carry the story, and the shadow on the study wall arrives as something noticed over the sewing before it becomes a terror.
characters.clue: Say that Henry had words with Edward the night before Edward died.

characters.name: Henry Glynn
characters.summary: He had words with Edward the night before Edward died, called the death gastric, and saw no need for an examination. When the shadow appears he moves every piece of furniture, then goes at the empty air with his father's old sword. He leaves for the city and does not come back.
characters.clue: Thrusts his father's sword through the space between the lamp and the wall.

characters.name: Grossmith, who is Manton
characters.role: The stranger in The Middle Toe of the Right Foot
characters.summary: He signs the hotel register as Robert Grossmith, takes offence on the porch and accepts a duel with knives in the dark in the old Manton house. The young men who arrange it know he is Manton, who cut the throats of his wife and two children in that house ten years before.
characters.clue: Is found dead in the corner, his knife dropped, with three lines of bare footprints leading towards him.
characters.firstAppearance: The Middle Toe of the Right Foot

relationships.label: each is undone in the room of his crime

characters.name: Miss Randolph
characters.role: The night nurse in The Shadowy Third
characters.summary: Young, Southern, just out of training and half in love with the surgeon who hires her. She sees his wife's dead daughter more than once and ends the story ready to swear on her deathbed to what she saw.
characters.clue: Sees a child's skipping-rope coiled on the stairs.

relationships.label: also sees what the man of the house denies

themes.name: What counts as proof
themes.summary: Bierce begins with testimony and ends with a footprint; Freeman's Henry tests the shadow by moving every piece of furniture; Dunbar's husband believes a message he cannot explain. Again and again the collection tests what a ghost story would need to convince anybody.
themes.development: The early stories rely on witnesses and objects; by Dunbar and Wharton belief is private, and the proof is what people do after it.

themes.name: Seven women among ten writers
themes.summary: Seven of the ten writers are women, and several of their stories turn on women noticing what the men of the house deny: Glasgow's nurse, Freeman's sisters, Mrs Rutledge in Bewitched.
themes.development: Crawford's story is told among men after dinner; the later ones centre on a nurse, a young bride, three sisters and a dead wife.

themes.name: The house as the haunted thing
themes.summary: Nearly every story is about a building: a state-room, a study, a room that may be a closet, a house that is not there, houses moved through the streets. The ghosts belong to places more than to people.
themes.development: The houses go from fixed and notorious in Bierce to unreliable in Wynne, Peattie and Dawson, until Dunbar's narrator is the house's memory of itself.

themes.name: The quarrel before the death
themes.summary: Several stories turn on something done shortly before a death and never admitted: a quarrel in a study, a duel arranged as a trick, a child's death her mother blames on her husband.
themes.development: No one is tried. The guilty die instead, and the stories leave open whether a ghost did it.

themes.name: What the dead still notice
themes.summary: Dunbar's narrator sees the unfilled gaps in her bookshelves and the disorder in her work-basket. The collection is unusually interested in the ordinary things a death leaves behind and who keeps them.
themes.development: Grief begins as possession — this is my room — and ends in The Shell of Sense as release.

themes.name: Who is allowed to tell it
themes.summary: A clubman's after-dinner yarn, a newspaper's certainty, a nurse ready to swear on her deathbed, a dead woman's first person. The form of the telling changes the ghost each time.
themes.development: Dunbar's story is told by the ghost herself, and in it the ghost does the kindest thing in the book.

techniques.name: The newspaper voice
techniques.definition: Reporting the supernatural in the flat register of a local news item.
techniques.inThisBook: Bierce opens by calling the haunting well known and dismissing doubters as cranks. The mock-official tone makes the house's reputation a fact before anything has happened in it.

techniques.name: A ghost as narrator
techniques.definition: Giving the story to a teller whose position no reader can check.
techniques.inThisBook: Dunbar's narrator is dead, jealous and certain of her rights to the house. The story works because she gradually becomes less reliable to herself and more generous to everyone else.

techniques.name: Small domestic proof
techniques.definition: A household object that carries the story's meaning.
techniques.inThisBook: A work-basket in disorder, gaps in a bookshelf, a shadow on a study wall, footprints in dust, a skipping-rope on the stairs. The evidence is usually something a housekeeper would notice first.

techniques.name: The last sentence
techniques.definition: Holding back the decisive fact until the very end.
techniques.inThisBook: Bierce's final line names the dead woman by her missing toe, and everything before it rearranges. Freeman ends on a telegram and never says what Henry did.

techniques.name: The yarn among friends
techniques.definition: A story presented as told aloud to an audience within the fiction.
techniques.inThisBook: Crawford's Upper Berth is told over cigars, after dinner, to men who have run out of conversation, which lets the teller admit how frightened he was.

techniques.name: American interiors
techniques.definition: The old haunted-house form set in newer, plainer rooms.
techniques.inThisBook: Studies, sickrooms, farmhouse closets, a steamship state-room, a shack on the plains. The haunted house has moved into ordinary American rooms.

quotations.text: “Henry had words with Edward in the study the night before Edward died,” said Caroline Glynn.
quotations.context: The first line of Freeman's story. Edward lies dead in the house.
quotations.analysis: Freeman opens a murder story in the grammar of a family complaint. Had words is exactly what a sister would say, and it puts the crime, if there is one, inside the ordinary vocabulary of a household quarrel.
quotations.source: Scarborough 1921 text, The Shadows on the Wall

quotations.text: Even the shock of death—for her brother Edward lay dead in the house—could not disturb her outward serenity of demeanor.
quotations.context: Describing Emma, the married sister and the family beauty, in her rocking-chair.
quotations.analysis: The dash drops the corpse into the middle of a sentence about composure. Freeman's comedy of manners is doing the work of a ghost story: the body in the house is a parenthesis to the sisters' self-possession.
quotations.source: Scarborough 1921 text, The Shadows on the Wall

quotations.text: “That strange shadow on the wall,” replied Mrs. Brigham.
quotations.context: Emma notices the shadow while sewing in the study; her sisters have seen it every night since Edward died.
quotations.analysis: It enters the story as something to remark on, and Caroline will not turn round to look. Freeman lets the reader work out that the shadow is old news to everyone in the room but Emma.
quotations.source: Scarborough 1921 text, The Shadows on the Wall

quotations.text: Not a line of its terrible outlines wavered.
quotations.context: Henry, a doctor, moves the study furniture to change the shadow.
quotations.analysis: A shadow that ignores the light is a contradiction stated as an observation. Henry has tested it like a scientist and the test has failed; from here his reasonableness starts to look like fear.
quotations.source: Scarborough 1921 text, The Shadows on the Wall

quotations.text: It is well known that the old Manton house is haunted.
quotations.reference: The Middle Toe of the Right Foot
quotations.context: The first sentence of Bierce's story.
quotations.analysis: Well known is the phrase of a man who has not checked. Bierce starts in the voice of local consensus so that the story's end can show what the consensus missed.
quotations.source: Scarborough 1921 text, The Middle Toe of the Right Foot

quotations.text: incredulity is confined to those opinionated persons who will be called “cranks” as soon as the useful word shall have penetrated the intellectual demesne of the Marshall Advance
quotations.reference: The Middle Toe of the Right Foot
quotations.context: Continuing the case for the haunting.
quotations.analysis: Bierce mocks the sceptics and the local paper in one sentence, and the joke is aimed at everybody. The reader is invited to side with neither, which is the right position for the ending.
quotations.source: Scarborough 1921 text, The Middle Toe of the Right Foot

quotations.text: The evidence that the house is haunted is of two kinds; the testimony of disinterested witnesses who have had ocular proof, and that of the house itself.
quotations.reference: The Middle Toe of the Right Foot
quotations.context: Setting out the case like a lawyer.
quotations.analysis: The house is called as a witness. The legal parody is funny, and it also tells you exactly how the story will be solved: by what the house kept, whatever anyone saw.
quotations.source: Scarborough 1921 text, The Middle Toe of the Right Foot

quotations.text: “The middle toe is missing—it was Gertrude!”
quotations.reference: The Middle Toe of the Right Foot
quotations.context: The last line, spoken by Gertrude's brother over the bare footprints in the dust.
quotations.analysis: The detail was planted on the hotel porch, where King admits he once threw over a girl who had lost a toe. It returns as identification. Bierce's method in one line: the supernatural is proved by a physical oddity, and the reader supplies the rest.
quotations.source: Scarborough 1921 text, The Middle Toe of the Right Foot

quotations.text: It was intolerably unchanged, the dim, dark-toned room.
quotations.context: The first sentence of Dunbar's story, spoken by the dead narrator.
quotations.analysis: Intolerably is the word that tells you who is speaking: only someone who has left could find sameness unbearable. The ghost’s first feeling is a housekeeper’s discomfort at a room that has carried on without her.
quotations.source: Scarborough 1921 text, The Shell of Sense

quotations.text: the very gaps that I myself had left in my bookshelves still stood unfilled
quotations.analysis: The dead notice absences. Dunbar gives her ghost an exact, bookish observation — the gaps are hers, and nobody has closed them — so that grief is described from the side of the person grieved for.
quotations.source: Scarborough 1921 text, The Shell of Sense

quotations.text: my work-basket was in disorder; it was preposterous that so small a thing should hurt me so
quotations.context: One of the first signs that her sister has taken her place.
quotations.analysis: The jealousy of the whole story arrives through a sewing basket. Dunbar makes the smallest domestic change carry the largest loss, and lets the narrator be embarrassed by her own feeling.
quotations.source: Scarborough 1921 text, The Shell of Sense

quotations.context: The first words of the final section, after she has brought her husband and her sister together.
quotations.analysis: Three words, after pages of possessive watching. The ghost gets out not by being laid to rest by the living but by letting them go, which reverses the usual direction of the form.
quotations.source: Scarborough 1921 text, The Shell of Sense

quotations.text: Theirs is the fullest joy that the dwellers in the shell of sense can know. Mine is the transcendent joy of the unseen spaces.
quotations.context: The last sentences of the story.
quotations.analysis: The title phrase comes back. Halfway through, Frances used it in a line of verse for the living, pitying them; now it names the happiness she is leaving them to. Dunbar gives her ghost the last word and a larger joy than anyone left in the room.
quotations.source: Scarborough 1921 text, The Shell of Sense

criticalViews.position: The magazine ghost story as a women's form
criticalViews.summary: Seven of the ten writers are women, and their stories put domestic observation at the centre: rooms, work-baskets, shadows, sickbeds. The magazines gave them a paid outlet and a subject they knew better than anyone.
criticalViews.counter: The magazines bought ghost stories from men on the same terms, and Crawford and Bierce are domestic in their own way: a cabin and an empty house.

criticalViews.summary: Nearly every story is organised around what would count as evidence: testimony, footprints, a shadow that ignores the lamp. Read together they are a set of experiments in belief.
criticalViews.counter: The strongest stories, Dunbar's and Wharton's, give up on proof and are interested in what belief lets people do.

criticalViews.summary: In 1905 Dunbar argued in The Dial that the ghost had declined in American magazine fiction. Three years later she published The Shell of Sense in Harper's.
criticalViews.counter: Most of the stories here were printed after 1890, which suggests the magazines kept buying ghosts; what changed was where they were set and who saw them.

criticalViews.summary: Scarborough's anthologies and later critics brought back several of these writers after they had dropped out of print.
criticalViews.counter: Wharton and Bierce never left print; what was rediscovered was the company they kept.

essayQuestions.question: How do these stories make a ghost believable?
essayQuestions.focus: Evidence, testimony and the physical detail
plan: Take Bierce's legal parody — testimony and the house itself — as the collection's own account of proof.
Examine the shadow in Freeman's study, which no moving of lamp or furniture will shift.
Set the footprints at the end of Bierce against it.
Turn to Dunbar, where proof is replaced by a message two people receive.
Conclude on which kind of evidence the book trusts most.

essayQuestions.question: What does it change to tell a ghost story from the ghost's side?
essayQuestions.focus: Narration in The Shell of Sense
plan: Describe the narrator's first observations: an unchanged room, gaps in the bookshelves, a work-basket in disorder.
Trace her jealousy of her sister and her attachment to the house.
Examine the turn: the message in the night, and the choice she makes.
Compare her with the ghosts other stories describe from outside.
Argue for what the reversal adds to the form.

essayQuestions.question: Why are so many of the houses unreliable?
plan: List the houses: a state-room, a derelict farmhouse, a room that is sometimes a closet, a house that is not there, houses moved through San Francisco's streets.
Consider what the American setting — new building, moving populations — does to the haunted-house tradition.
Use Freeman and Dunbar to show the house as a woman's domain.
Weigh the comic and the frightening uses of the unstable house.
Conclude on what the collection suggests about home.

discussionQuestions: Bierce calls the haunting well known. Who, in these stories, gets to decide what is known?
Frances says she had not known how greatly Allan could love. Is The Shell of Sense about jealousy, or about how little she knew him?
Seven of the ten writers are women. Would you have guessed which seven from the stories alone?
Freeman never says what Henry did. Do you need to know?
Which story frightened you most, and is it the one with the most evidence or the least?
Why do so many of these ghosts belong to rooms, and not to people?
